Good infrastructure requires the proper mix of power-generating technologies.  Example, the sun doesn't shine at night (and house-sized batteries are damned expensive) whereas the wind frequently does blow at night.  Therefore, even if less efficient ("profitable"), wind technology should likely be part of the equation.

The same can be said for ocean and geothermal (nuclear is a special case). But non-renewable electric power has little future in Hawaii since we utterly lack coal, oil and all other non-renewable energy resources.

Comment: "how deep are these lines ??"

Minimum depth of cover is usually 0.60 m (2 feet), deeper than that under roads & railways & river crossings. 

As for deeper being better, that would be true re. load from above the pipe. But the operating pressures in transmission pipelines are so high (usually over 500 psi and often over 1,000 psi) that a major release will blow off the ground cover at almost any reasonable depth.

Also, the deeper the pipe is the longer it will take to detect a smaller leak. Pinhole leaks are notoriously difficult to detect and can cause considerable environmental and legal headaches.

I was stunned when I observed an excavated pipeline in Kingston: it looked like less than 2' of cover to me but I didn't have a tape measure with me. But the cover was almost entirely limestone rubble. I expected that pipelines would be backfilled with several inches of sand or other soft fill, not rocks. This 1952 pipeline carries mostly gasoline and usually runs at 1,200 psi.
